questions.question: Which four conditions must all hold for a deadlock?
options: Starvation, aging, priority and preemption
Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait
Mutual exclusion, paging, swapping and circular wait
questions.why: Take away any one of the four (for example, allow preemption) and a deadlock cannot form.

questions.question: What does the wait-for graph show when the lot is deadlocked?
options: A cycle: each car waits for the next, and the last waits for the first
A single car with no arrows
Arrows that all point to the exit
questions.why: A cycle in the wait-for graph is exactly a circular wait, so detection looks for cycles.

questions.question: Towing a car to break the jam is which recovery method?
options: Adding more resources
Avoidance with the Banker's algorithm
Preemption: taking a resource away from a process
questions.why: The towed car loses its bay (its resource), which lets the others move again.

questions.question: When does the Banker's algorithm grant a request?
options: Whenever enough bays are free right now
Only if the system is still in a safe state afterwards
Only for the fleet with the smallest need
questions.why: Free bays are not enough: after granting, there must still be an order in which every fleet can finish.

questions.question: How is a fleet's Need worked out?
options: Max minus Allocation
Allocation minus Available
Max plus Available
questions.why: Need is what a fleet may still ask for: its declared maximum minus what it already holds.

questions.question: What does it mean for the state to be safe?
options: No fleet is waiting at the moment
Every bay is free
There is some order in which every fleet can get its maximum and finish
questions.why: That order is the safe sequence the safety check searches for.

questions.question: Which algorithm can take the CPU away when a shorter job arrives?
options: First come, first served
Shortest remaining time first
Non-preemptive priority
questions.why: SRTF is preemptive: it always runs the process with the least work left.

questions.question: A process's waiting time is…
options: its turnaround time minus its burst time
its completion time minus its arrival time
its burst time minus its arrival time
questions.why: Turnaround is the whole stay in the system; take away the time spent running and what remains is waiting.

questions.question: What does Round Robin give each process?
options: The CPU until it finishes
A share based only on its priority
A fixed time slice (quantum), in turn
questions.why: When the quantum runs out, the process goes to the back of the ready queue: fair to everyone.

questions.question: When does a page fault happen?
options: When the page the program needs is not in any frame
When a frame is empty
When two pages have the same number
questions.why: The page must then be brought in from disk, which is slow: that is why fewer faults is better.

questions.question: Which page does FIFO evict?
options: The one used least recently
The one that has been in memory the longest
The one needed furthest in the future
questions.why: First in, first out: the oldest arrival leaves, even if it is used often.

questions.question: Which policy has the fewest faults, but cannot be built in a real system?
options: LRU
FIFO
Optimal
questions.why: Optimal needs to know the future reference string; it is the yardstick the others are measured against.
